note: Europe at the end of 1945. Germany and Austria were divided into Allied occupation zones; the Baltic states were incorporated into the Soviet Union; Czechoslovakia was restored; and Albania, Bulgaria, Finland, Poland and Romania reflected postwar territorial changes. Berlin and Vienna are shown as whole regions rather than divided sectors, and modern administrative regions are approximate proxies for several unsettled borders.

properties.label: Soviet Zone
properties.info: The Soviet occupation zone in Germany, including Berlin as a whole-region proxy for its four postwar sectors.

properties.label: British Zone
properties.info: The British occupation zone in Germany, shown with modern state boundaries as approximate proxies.

properties.label: US Zone
properties.info: The United States occupation zone in Germany. The combined modern Baden-Wurttemberg region is assigned as a broad proxy.

properties.label: French Zone
properties.info: The French occupation zone in Germany, approximated by modern Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland.
The Soviet occupation zone in Austria. Vienna is shown whole in this zone because the map has no sector-level city polygons.
The United States occupation zone in Austria, approximated by modern Upper Austria and Salzburg.
The British occupation zone in Austria, approximated by modern Carinthia and Styria.
The French occupation zone in Austria, approximated by modern Tyrol and Vorarlberg.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had been occupied and annexed by the Soviet Union. Modern administrative regions are used as proxies.
Soviet postwar gains include northern East Prussia, Bessarabia, the Karelian territories and Carpathian Ruthenia; modern regions are approximate.

properties.leader: Charles de Gaulle (President of the Provisional Government)

properties.label: Albania
properties.info: Albania was governed by Enver Hoxha's Democratic Government at the end of 1945.
